title: The electrochemical production of C2/C3 species from carbon dioxide on copper-modified boron-doped diamond electrodes
abstract: We report on the first observation of the production of C2/C3 species from the electrochemical reduction of CO2 at the surfaces of copper-modified borondoped diamond (Cu-BDD) electrodes in aqueous media at room temperature and ambient pressure. The product distribution is dependent on the amount of deposited Cu and the applied potential. At low potential, -1.0 V (vs. Ag/AgCl), ethanol was observed as the main product with acetaldehyde and acetone as side products. The highest faradaic efficiencies obtained for ethanol, acetaldehyde and acetone were 42.4%, 13.7% and 7%, respectively. The Cu particles on the surfaces of the BDD electrodes remained stable, showing insignificant differences after the CO2 electroreduction process under these particular conditions. The efficiency dropped with increasing Cu deposition time and at high reduction potentials. Moreover, we present comparisons with a Cu M AN US CR IP T AC CE PT ED ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT 2 plate and Cu-modified glassy carbon as working electrodes under the same conditions, which explains the specific behavior of the CO2 reduction process on the Cu-BDD electrode.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
During the last few decades, the electrochemical reduction of CO2 for the production of valuable fuels and commodity chemicals has been widely studied, especially for those compounds with a higher number of carbon atoms from which the production of ready-to-use fuel can be developed. However, direct transfer of electrons to the CO2 molecules requires a high overpotential. There have been many attempts to develop a suitable catalyst by using, for example, a metal complex,1,2 bioelectrocatalyst,3,4 direct electrochemical reduction using a metal catalyst,5-7 or by using carbon-based electrodes.8,9
The electrochemical properties of BDD electrodes are excellent, in that they have a wide potential window and low background current. Moreover, they are chemically inert and mechanically durable, and have been widely used for electroanalysis, electrocatalyst, and electrosynthesis applications.10-12 With regard to the electrochemical reduction of CO2, the wide potential window of BDD electrodes gives them the advantage of being able to improve the selectivity of the electrochemical reduction process against the generation of hydrogen as an unwanted competing

side product. The direct electrochemical reduction of CO2 on BDD electrodes has been investigated.13-16 Moreover, several studies on the electrochemical reduction of CO2 using modified BDD electrodes have been reported.17-19 So far, the main products have been carbon monoxide, formaldehyde, formic acid, and methanol. However, high carbon-containing compounds have not yet been observed.
It is expected that the electrocatalytic activity and the selectivity of BDD electrodes can be improved by modifying the surface. At present, Cu is the best-known metal catalyst for the electrochemical reduction of CO2, and has the capability to produce many different products, especially hydrocarbons and even oxygenated species.20-21 Therefore, we modified BDD electrodes with Cu nanoparticles and, using these electrodes, studied the production of higher carbon-containing compounds. We also examined the effect of lowering the required overpotential on the rate of CO2 reduction with these electrodes. In this paper, we report on the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to ethanol (the main product), acetaldehyde and acetone (other C2 and C3 species), which were successfully produced at low potential on Cu-BDD electrodes.

sections.heading: 2.2 Preparation of the working electrodes
sections.text:
BDD films were deposited onto Si (111) wafers using a microwave
plasma-assisted chemical vapor deposition system (Model AX 5400, CORNES Technology Corp.). The details of the preparation are described elsewhere.20 Electrodeposition of Cu nanoparticles on BDD electrodes were carried out in 10 ml of 0.1 M H2SO4 containing a 1 mM CuSO4 aqueous solution at -0.6 V (vs. Ag/AgCl). The deposition potential was determined by cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurement in a CuSO4 solution on a BDD electrode (Figure S1A). The deposition times were 50 s (Cu-BDD-50), 100 s (Cu-BDD-100), and 300 s (CuBDD-300) (Figure S1B). N2 gas purging was performed for 5 minutes prior to electrodeposition to remove the dissolved oxygen.23 The Cu-BDD electrodes were then rinsed with water and dried at room temperature and pressure for 1 hour, followed by ultrasonication in water for about 5 minutes and dried under N2 gas. Moreover, the modified electrodes were recovered by immersion in an aqua regia solution for 10 minutes followed by ultrasonication in ultrapure water for 15 minutes. Electrode characterization was performed using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (JCM6000, JEOL) before and after electrolysis.

sections.heading: 2.3 Methods
sections.text:
The electrochemical measurements were conducted in a cell with two
compartments separated by a Nafion membrane (Figure S2). A 0.5 M KCl
M AN
US CR
IP T

solution was used as the catholyte, and a 0.5 M KOH solution as the anolyte (15 mL in each cell).24 Cu-BDD, a Pt mesh, and Ag/AgCl were used as the working, counter, and reference electrodes, respectively. The geometric area of the working electrode in the contact with electrolyte was 0.754 cm2. Prior to electrochemical reduction, the catholyte side was purged with N2 gas for 5 minutes, followed by CO2 bubbling for 15 minutes. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was performed with a scan rate of 20 mV/s in the potential range from 0 V to -1.8 V (vs. Ag/AgCl). The electrochemical reduction of CO2 was conducted for 2 hours at potentials ranging from -0.8 V to -1.2 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) at room temperature and pressure. The liquid products were analyzed using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GCMS-QP2010 Ultra, Shimadzu Corp.) by the autoinjection headspace method (5 mL sample in 20 mL volume vial) with the selected ion monitoring (SIM) mode for the target products, and also using high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) with electroconductivity and UV/Vis detectors (Prominence, Shimadzu Corp.). The gas products were analyzed by gas chromatography with a flame ionization detector and a thermal conductivity detector (GC-2014, Shimadzu Corp.).

As the deposition time becomes longer, the potential window becomes narrower. Figure 2B shows XPS spectra before and after Cu deposition on BDD surface. The peaks at binding energy of 932.05 and 952 eV correspond to Cu 2p3/2 and Cu 2p1/2, respectively (Figure 2C). The Cu/C ratio was 0.08. Furthermore, the O/C ratio after Cu deposition (0.09) was larger than that before Cu deposition (0.006). These results explain that not only Cu but also some oxide species were formed after the Cu deposition on the surface of BDD electrode. In addition, since BDD cannot be oxidized at potential -0.6 V (vs Ag/AgCl) where the Cu is deposited, the detected oxygen seems to derive from the oxide form of Cu. Figure 3A-F (additional pictures in Figure S5A-F) show the SEM images before and after CO2 electroreduction for 2 hours at -1.0 V (vs. Ag/AgCl). The average sizes of the Cu particles on the Cu-BDD electrode surfaces were around 50-85 nm (Figure S3). However, on the Cu-BDD-300 electrode surface, accumulation of the Cu particles made it easy for them to become detached. On the other hand, the SEM images of the Cu-BDD-100 surface before and after electroreduction show insignificant differences, indicating the Cu-BDD had remained stable.

Figure 3G shows the efficiencies with which ethanol, acetone, and
acetaldehyde were produced by reduction at -1.0 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) for 2 hours at room temperature and pressure. The highest faradaic efficiencies for ethanol, acetaldehyde, and acetone are 42.4 %, 13.7%, and 7%, respectively, which were obtained with the Cu-BDD-100 electrode. With the Cu-BDD-50 electrode, the amount of Cu nanoparticles was insufficient to react with CO2 effectively. In fact, bare BDD electrode without Cu could not generate any products at such low potential, except hydrogen. Therefore, the faradaic efficiencies become lower on Cu-BDD-50 than on Cu-BDD-100. However, for Cu deposition times of more than 100 s, the efficiency dropped due to the instability of the Cu nanoparticles deposited on the BDD surface (Figure 3G). It can be explained that as the Cu nanoparticle accumulated on the surface of BDD electrode, the potential window becomes narrower and tend to increase hydrogen evolution, which may detach the Cu nanoparticles on the surface of BDD electrode and thus decrease the efficiency of CO2 electrochemical reduction. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that C2/C3 species have been produced with reasonable efficiency by the electrochemical reduction of CO2 using a modified BDD electrode. Moreover, ethanol is well known to be widely used as solvent, feedstock, and even as a fuel.
Since the best performance was achieved with the Cu-BDD-100 electrode,

The highest faradaic efficiency for the production of ethanol was achieved at -1.0 V (vs. Ag/AgCl). The repeatability of the amount produced is indicated by the standard deviation obtained from three different experiments at this potential for 2 hours (Figure S4). From Figure 4A, we can see a significant decline in the faradaic efficiency for the production of ethanol at more negative potential than - 1.0 V (vs. Ag/AgCl), which might be due to the high production of hydrogen gas detaching Cu nanoparticles from the surface of the electrode. This can also be explained by referring to Figure 4B, in which the current vs. time profiles for the reduction of CO2 at different potentials are plotted, and which shows that, at more negative potential than -1.0 V (vs. Ag/AgCl), there are large changes in current density with time. Moreover, the differences on the BDD surfaces can be seen from the SEM images after 2 hours reduction at various potentials (Figure S5). After reduction at -1.2 V (vs. Ag/AgCl), the Cu nanoparticles had become detached, and the Cu nanoparticles remaining on the surface became smaller on average by about 50 nm. On the other hand, at more positive potential than -1.0 V (vs. Ag/AgCl), the Cu nanoparticles seemed to have been stable. Moreover, the production efficiency of acetone increased as the

On the bare BDD electrode, CO2 electrochemical reduction proceeds at more highly negative potential.15 On the Cu electrode, considering the potential dependence, we carried out experiments with the Cu electrode at -1.6 V (vs. Ag/AgCl), resulting in the production of ethanol, acetone, acetaldehyde, and formic acid with faradaic efficiencies of less than 1%. On the other hand, the production was dominated by the evolution of hydrogen gas and a small amount of CO gas. This is in line with previous reports21,25 showing that, with a bare Cu electrode, a high overpotential was required to produce hydrocarbons or multicarbon oxygenated species. On the other hand, at low potential, hydrogen production dominates. However, this behavior was not found with the Cu-BDD electrodes, where ethanol, acetaldehyde, and acetone were produced at low potentials of -1.0 V (vs. Ag/AgCl). This suggests that the nanosized Cu particles deposited on the surface of the BDD electrodes have high affinity, and tend, therefore, to interact more efficiently with the CO2 molecules and their intermediates.
Studies of the production of C2 at the surfaces of Cu electrodes have, so
far, only been observed on rough surfaces, such as those produced by electrodeposition or after a thermal pretreatment.26-28 Besides, to produce higher carbon-containing products such as C2/C3 species, C-C coupling reactions are needed during reduction.29 C-C coupling reactions are strongly influenced by the amount of CO bound to the surface of the electrode, which influences the CO-CO coupling or the coupling with other hydrogenated intermediates. Vollmer et al. 30 reported that CO binds more strongly with

These studies clearly show that rough surfaces are needed to increase the adsorption of CO, and thus promote C-C coupling reactions.
On Cu-BDD electrodes, the formation of C2/C3 products is at a low
potential (-1.0 V). This can be explained by the fact that at more negative potentials, electron and proton transfer are more favorable, thus the intermediate C1 species on the surface of the electrode are likely to desorb as C1 products (i.e. CO, CH4, HCOOH, etc.) rather than remain and couple with other intermediates to form higher carbon-containing compounds. In fact, in these days, bioelectrochemical approaches for CO2 reduction using microorganisms are reported.3,4,31,32 Although routine CO2 reduction is possible at lower potential, that needs more complicated and very specific condition because of the use of living organisms. Furthermore, the yield of the products is not stable. It is also in line with our previously reported results for the electroreduction of CO2 to HCOOH on a bare BDD electrode, which took place by reduction at high potential.15 Indeed, a more detailed understanding of the mechanism is worth further study.
For comparison with other carbon-based electrodes, the electroreduction
of CO2 with glassy carbon (GC) and Cu-modified GC (Cu-GC) electrodes was also conducted at -1.0 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) for 2 hours (Figure S6). As a result, on both electrodes, hydrogen evolution dominated. At the same time, the efficiency

In conclusion, the production of C2/C3 species is feasible on a relatively
inert BDD electrode by modifying it with Cu. In this work, BDD electrode seems to play a role as a stable supporting electrode which suppress the hydrogen evolution. Previously, Roy et al. 19 reported a study on a copper-modified BDD electrode in aqueous ionic liquid. Nonetheless, products higher than C1 species were not reported and they were dominated by hydrogen gas. Despite using similarly modified electrodes, the higher potentials applied and the bigger sizes and greater amounts of Cu particles, which promote faster electron and proton transfer, may be the reasons for this. Recently, Song et al. 33 reported ethanol production on a Cu nanoparticle/N-doped graphene electrode. The reaction pathway, however, remains in question, and although similar behavior was shown using a doped material, the other benefit of using BDD electrodes is that they are highly durable and promising for real applications. Moreover, using BDD electrodes, C3 species, which were not observed by Song et al., were observed for the first time. The future challenge is to develop procedures for the reduction of CO2 to high carbon-containing compounds.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
The electrochemical reduction of CO2 on Cu-BDD electrodes was
successfully carried out, producing C2/C3 species with high efficiency at low reduction potentials. The Cu deposited on the electrodes remained stable,

showing insignificant differences after 2 hours reduction at -1.0 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) or less. The wide potential window of BDD seems to be responsible for suppressing the production of hydrogen compared to a glassy carbon electrode. So far, the effective current density for production of C2/C3 species is low, which is probably due to the small amount of Cu nanoparticles. Therefore, in the next step, we will investigate the electrochemical CO2 reduction on a BDD electrode modified with a larger amount of Cu nanoparticles whose size, distribution, and stability should be the same as this work. The production of 2/C3 species will give impetus to further studies using BDD electrodes to possibly produce high carbon-containing compounds with certain types of catalyst.
